  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.ValidateOwner
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: normalize

normalize:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.NormalizeOwnerTelephone
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: ensureUniqueTelephone

  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: ensureUniqueHousehold

  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.EnsureUniqueHousehold
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: build

build:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.BuildOwner
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: assignCustomerCode

assignCustomerCode:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.AssignCustomerCode
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: assignHousehold

assignHousehold:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.AssignHousehold
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: save

save:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.SaveOwner
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: respond

respond:
  class: org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.owner.RespondWithOwnerCreated
  govern: [ transaction ]

content.text:
VERDICT: CHANGES REQUESTED

The new logic is wired in at a sensible point and the class is appropriately scoped, but it introduces duplication that this codebase already has an established, better pattern for.

**Finding 1 — `normalize(String)` is duplicated verbatim, and the codebase already shows the idiomatic fix.**
`AssignHousehold.normalize` is a byte-for-byte copy of `EnsureUniqueHousehold.normalize` (trim → collapse whitespace → lower-case). The author even documents the coupling in prose — the class javadoc says "compared … matching `EnsureUniqueHousehold`" — which is a strong signal the shared rule wants to live in code, not in a comment that a future maintainer can silently break. These two must stay identical for correctness: the owner that `EnsureUniqueHousehold` lets through on `sharesHousehold` must be matched by `AssignHousehold` using the *same* comparison semantics. If one `normalize` ever diverges, an owner is admitted to a household but assigned no/other household members.

The codebase already solves exactly this: `OwnerEmails` is a package-private `final` helper described as the "single source of truth for what a 'normalized' owner email is," shared across steps. Follow that precedent — extract a `Households` (or similar) helper in this package holding the shared `normalize`, and let both `EnsureUniqueHousehold` and `AssignHousehold` delegate to it.

**Finding 2 — the household-match predicate is duplicated too.**
Both classes carry the same `lastName.equals(normalize(existing.getLastName())) && address.equals(normalize(existing.getAddress()))` loop condition — the definition of "same household." That predicate is the real shared concept and belongs next to the shared `normalize` (e.g. a `sameHousehold(Owner, lastName, address)` helper), so the uniqueness check and the back-fill can't drift apart.

Note `deriveHouseholdId` is reasonably local to `AssignHousehold` (nothing else needs it) and is fine where it is; the concern is specifically the matching/normalization logic that now exists in two places.
